items.stem: What term is commonly used in Hindi for a market, especially a weekly or local one?

options.label: A
options.text: Bazaar or Haat

options.label: B
options.text: Mandi or Chowk

options.label: C
options.text: Dukaan or Gali

options.label: D
options.text: Kendra or Sadan

items.answer:  (A) Bazaar or Haat In Hindi, a market is often referred to as a ‘bazaar’. A local or weekly market, particularly in rural or semi-urban areas, is commonly called a ‘haat’.

items.stem: How does an online market primarily differ from a physical market regarding buyer-seller interaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Online markets have much lower prices

options.label: B
options.text: Physical markets offer a wider variety goods

options.label: C
options.text: Buyers and sellers need not meet in person

options.label: D
options.text: Only physical markets use monetary payments

items.answer:  (C) Buyers and sellers need not meet in person In a physical market, buyers and sellers interact directly in person. In an online market, transactions occur remotely through websites or apps, so buyers and sellers do not need to meet physically.

items.stem: If a seller sets the price of guavas too high (e.g., `80/kg when buyers expect much less), what is the likely immediate outcome in the market?

options.label: A
options.text: All guavas will sell out very quickly

options.label: B
options.text: Many buyers may not be willing to buy

options.label: C
options.text: The seller will make a very large profit

options.label: D
options.text: Other sellers will also raise their prices

items.answer:  (B) Many buyers may not be willing to buy If a seller prices a product significantly higher than what buyers perceive as reasonable or are willing to pay, many potential buyers will likely refrain from purchasing, leading to low sales for that seller.

items.stem: In the chain of supply, _____ buy goods in large quantities from producers and sell them to retailers.

options.label: A
options.text: consumers

options.label: B
options.text: distributors

options.label: C
options.text: wholesalers

options.label: D
options.text: advertisers

items.answer:  (C) wholesalers Wholesalers are intermediaries who purchase goods in bulk directly from manufacturers or producers. They sell these goods in smaller quantities to retailers, who in turn sell to end consumers.

items.stem: What are specialized warehouses designed to maintain specific low temperatures for preserving perishable goods like fruits and vegetables called?

options.label: A
options.text: Godowns for all

options.label: B
options.text: Silos types

options.label: C
options.text: Cold storage

options.label: D
options.text: Granaries type

items.answer:  (C) Cold storage Cold storage facilities are specialized warehouses equipped with refrigeration systems to maintain low temperatures. This controlled environment helps preserve perishable items like fruits, vegetables, and dairy products, extending their shelf life.

items.stem: A garment store offers a 50% discount on all woolen sweaters at the end of the winter season. What is the most likely reason for this price reduction strategy used?

options.label: A
options.text: The sweaters have become very low quality

options.label: B
options.text: To clear out seasonal stock for new items

options.label: C
options.text: Wool prices have fallen sharply in market

options.label: D
options.text: The government has ordered price cuts

items.answer:  (B) To clear out seasonal stock for new items Retailers often offer significant discounts on seasonal items like woolen sweaters at the end of winter to clear out the remaining stock. This makes space for new season’s merchandise and minimizes losses on unsold seasonal goods.

items.stem: What is a ‘retailer’ in the market chain?

options.label: A
options.text: Someone who produces goods in large factory

options.label: B
options.text: One who buys goods in bulk from producer

options.label: C
options.text: A shopkeeper selling goods to final consumer

options.label: D
options.text: A person who transports goods between cities

items.answer:  (C) A shopkeeper selling goods to final consumer A retailer is a business or person that sells goods directly to the final consumers for their own use or consumption, rather than for resale. items.stem: What are the main features of a market? Recall a recent visit to a market to purchase a product. What are the different features of a market that you observed during this visit?
items.answer:  Main features : Buyers, sellers, goods/services for exchange, and an agreed-upon price. (Observation from visit depends on personal experience). Example : “At the vegetable market, I (buyer) saw vendors (sellers) with produce (goods). I asked the price of tomatoes, bargained slightly, agreed on a price, and bought 1 kg.”

items.stem: Remember the epigraph from a famous economist at the beginning of the chapter? Discuss its relevance in the context of the chapter you have read.
items.answer:  The epigraph by Adam Smith states that prosperity comes from markets where people exchange goods/services they can’t create themselves. This is relevant as the chapter explains how markets (physical/online, wholesale/retail) facilitate this exchange, fulfilling needs/wants and driving economic activity. items.stem: Have you heard about or visited a school carnival/ fair organized by your school or any other school? Discuss with your friends and teachers about the kind of activities organized by students there. How do they conduct selling and negotiation with the buyers?
items.answer:  Students typically set up stalls for games, food, or handmade crafts. Selling involv1\es setting prices, attracting customers, and sometimes engaging in friendly negotiation, especially for crafts or games with prizes.

items.stem: Choose any 5 products and check out the label with the certification signs discussed in the chapter. Did you find products that did not have a logo? Why do you think this is so?
items.answer:  Students might find logos like FSSAI on food, ISI on appliances, AGMARK on spices, or BEE stars on electronics. Products without logos might be locally made unbranded items, handicrafts, or items where certification isn’t mandatory or common (e.g., loose vegetables, some clothing).

items.stem: You and your classmates have manufactured a soap bar. Design a label for its packaging. What in your opinion should be mentioned on the label for the consumer to know the product better?
items.answer:  A label should include : Brand Name, Product Name (e.g., “Handmade Neem Soap”), Key Ingredients, Net Weight, Manufacturer’s Name & Address, Manufacturing Date, Expiry Date/ Best Before, MRP (Maximum Retail Price), and potentially benefits (e.g., “Moisturizing,” “Antibacterial”) or certifications (if applicable). MULT IPL E CHOICE QUESTIO 

items.stem: What is a ‘market’ in its most basic sense?

options.label: A
options.text: A place only for social gatherings

options.label: B
options.text: A place where people buy and sell

options.label: C
options.text: A government office for collecting many taxes

options.label: D
options.text: A historical site with ancient old ruins

items.answer:  (B) A place where people buy and sell A market, in its fundamental sense, is any place, whether physical or online, where buyers and sellers come together to exchange goods and services, typically involving a transaction with an agreed-upon price.

items.stem: The Hampi Bazaar, a prosperous market in the 16th century, was part of which South Indian empire?

options.label: A
options.text: The Chola Empire

options.label: B
options.text: The Pallava Empire

options.label: C
options.text: The Vijayanagara Empire

options.label: D
options.text: The Chalukya Empire

items.answer:  (C) The Vijayanagara Empire The Hampi Bazaar was a renowned and flourishing marketplace located within the Vijayanagara Empire in Karnataka. It served as a major center for trade during the 16th century and before.

items.stem: According to the Portuguese traveller Domingos Paes, what made Hampi “the best-provided city in the world”? year

options.label: A
options.text: Its advanced military and strong fortifications

options.label: B
options.text: The wide variety of products traded

options.label: C
options.text: Its beautiful temples and religious sites

options.label: D
options.text: The pleasant climate throughout the whole

items.answer:  (B) The wide variety of products traded Domingos Paes described Hampi as exceptionally well-provided due to the immense variety and abundance of goods traded in its markets. This included grains, silk, animals, precious stones, and many other commodities.

items.stem: What is ‘price’ in the context of a market transaction?

options.label: A
options.text: The physical quality of the goods sold

options.label: B
options.text: The location of the market or shop

options.label: C
options.text: The amount at which buyer and seller agree

options.label: D
options.text: The time of day the sale occurs

items.answer:  (C) The amount at which buyer and seller agree Price is the mutually agreed-upon amount of money that a buyer is willing to pay and a seller is willing to accept in exchange for a particular good or service in a market. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube

items.stem: What are ‘inputs for production’ in an economic context?

options.label: A
options.text: The final products sold to all consumers

options.label: B
options.text: The profits earned by a manufacturing firm

options.label: C
options.text: Materials or resources used in making goods

options.label: D
options.text: The advertisements used to promote product

items.answer:  (C) Materials or resources used in making goods Inputs for production are the raw materials, components, labor, capital, and other resources that are used in the process of creating goods or providing services in an economic system.

items.stem: The government setting a ‘minimum price’ for agricultural products like wheat ensures what for the farmers? price

options.label: A
options.text: They can sell unlimited quantities at high

options.label: B
options.text: They do not incur losses due to low price

options.label: C
options.text: They are exempt from paying any income tax

options.label: D
options.text: They receive free inputs for next crop

items.answer:  (B) They do not incur losses due to low price By setting a minimum support price (MSP) for certain agricultural products, the government aims to protect farmers from sharp falls in market prices and ensure they receive a baseline remuneration, preventing significant losses.

items.stem: Why does the government set an ‘upper limit’ on the prices of essential goods like lifesaving drugs? make more accessible

options.label: A
options.text: To encourage pharmaceutical companies to

options.label: B
options.text: To ensure these goods are affordable

options.label: C
options.text: To promote the export of these drugs

options.label: D
options.text: To increase tax revenue from their sale

items.answer:  (B) To ensure these goods are affordable, accessible The government imposes price ceilings (upper limits) on essential items like lifesaving drugs to prevent them from becoming exorbitantly expensive. This ensures that these critical goods remain affordable and accessible to the general public.

items.stem: During a particular season, the supply of onions in the market drastically reduces due to crop failure. According to basic market principles, what is the most likely immediate impact on the price of onions?

options.label: A
options.text: The price of onions will decrease significantly

options.label: B
options.text: The price of onions will remain unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: The price of onions will likely increase

options.label: D
options.text: The government will ban the sale of onions

items.answer:  (C) The price of onions will likely increase. When the supply of a commodity like onions decreases while demand remains relatively stable or increases, the price tends to rise. This is a fundamental principle of supply and demand in a market economy.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a primary role of the government in relation to markets ? goods

options.label: A
options.text: Controlling prices to protect buyers or sellers

options.label: B
options.text: Ensuring quality and safety standards for

options.label: C
options.text: Directly owning and operating all retail shops

options.label: D
options.text: Mitigating negative external effects of markets

items.answer:  (C) Directly owning and operating all retail shops While governments regulate markets, set standards, and provide public goods, directly owning and operating all retail shops is not a typical primary role in most market economies discussed. They may run some public distribution outlets.

items.stem: What role does an ‘aggregator’ (like a shopping app or website) play in online markets?

options.label: A
options.text: They manufacture all the products they sell

options.label: B
options.text: They provide loans to online buyers only

options.label: C
options.text: They organize offers from multiple sellers

options.label: D
options.text: They physically inspect every item before sale

items.answer:  (C) They organize offers from multiple sellers An aggregator in an online market is a platform (website or app) that brings together and organizes product or service offers from various sellers, presenting them to consumers in one convenient place for purchase.

items.stem: Surat, Gujarat, is famously known as a major hub for which industry, besides being Asia’s oldest textile market?

options.label: A
options.text: Automobile manufacturing parts

options.label: B
options.text: Diamond cutting and polishing

options.label: C
options.text: Software development service

options.label: D
options.text: Heavy machinery production

items.answer:  (B) Diamond cutting and polishing Apart from its extensive textile industry, Surat is a global center for the diamond industry, renowned for its large-scale diamond cutting and polishing activities, employing a vast number of artisans for this.

items.stem: Which type of market is correctly paired with its primary characteristic? national borders quantities to consumer physically

options.label: A
options.text: Domestic Market - Trade occurs across

options.label: B
options.text: Wholesale Market - Sells goods in small

options.label: C
options.text: Online Market - Buyers and sellers must meet

options.label: D
options.text: Retail Market - Sells goods to final consumers

items.answer:  (D) Retail Market - Sells goods to final consumers A retail market consists of businesses (retailers) that sell goods and services directly to end consumers for their personal use. Domestic markets are within a country, wholesale is bulk, and online markets don’t require physical meeting.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Markets facilitate transactions between producers and consumers. Reason (R) : Markets help individuals access goods and services they cannot produce themselves. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Markets indeed facilitate the exchange between producers and consumers. This is crucial because individuals and businesses rely on markets to obtain goods and services that they do not or cannot produce themselves.

items.stem: Which market term is INCORRECTLY defined? country to another. for own country. consumption . trade.

options.label: A

items.answer:  (C) Wholesaler - Buys small quantities for direct consumption . A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities (bulk) from producers or manufacturers, primarily for resale to retailers, not in small quantities for direct consumption. The other terms are correctly defined.

items.stem: The Hampi Bazaar was known for trading only locally made crafts. Which of the above statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

options.label: D
options.text: 1, 2 and 3

items.answer:  (A) 1 and 2 only Physical markets involve in-person interaction. Online markets facilitate remote transactions. The Hampi Bazaar was known for a wide variety of products, including goods from distant places, not just local crafts. Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart

items.stem: In the example of buying and selling of guavas, imagine that the seller is getting a good price, and is able to make a profit... What is the farmer likely to do in this kind of a situation? Do you think he will start thinking about the demand for guavas in the next season? What is likely to be his response?
items.answer:  If the farmer sees high demand and good prices for guavas (signaled through the seller), they are likely to try and grow more guavas in the next season to increase their own earnings. Yes, they will likely anticipate continued demand based on the current market signals.

items.stem: Match the following types of markets with their characteristics : Markets Criteria 1 Physical market Goods and services flow outside the nation’s boundaries 2 Online market Deals in bulk quantities 3 Domestic market Serves the final consumers with goods and services 4 International market Requires physical presence of buyers and seller 5 Wholesale market Buyers and sellers meet virtually and can transact at any time 6 Retail market Lies within the boundaries of a nation

Prices are generally determined by the interaction between demand from buyers and supply by sellers. Can you think of products where prices are high despite lesser number of buyers demanding the product? What could be the reasons for that?
items.answer:  Yes, examples include luxury goods (designer handbags, high-end cars), rare collectibles (art, antiques), or highly specialized equipment. Reasons include high production costs, scarcity/ rarity, brand value/status symbol, or very specific niche demand where buyers are willing to pay a premium.

items.stem: Look at the real life situation that a retail seller of vegetables encountered... A family came to shop for vegetables. The price of beans that the seller on the cart was offering was `30/kg. The lady started to bargain with the seller to bring the price down to `25 / kg. The seller protested and refused to sell at that price saying he would make a loss at that price. The lady walks away. The family goes to a super bazaar nearby. They buy vegetables in the super bazaar where they pay `40 / kg for the beans that is neatly packed in a plastic bag. What are the reasons that the family does this? Are there factors that affect buying and selling which are not directly connected to price?
items.answer:  The family might prefer the super bazaar for perceived quality, better hygiene, convenience (multiple items in one place), fixed prices (no bargaining needed), or better packaging, even if the price is higher. Yes, factors beyond price include convenience, quality perception, shopping environment, brand trust, and packaging.

items.stem: There are some districts in India that are famous for growing tomatoes. However, during some seasons, the situation is not good for farmers. With a large quantity of harvest, there are reports of farmers throwing away their produce and all their hard work going to waste. Why do you think farmers do this? What role can wholesalers play in such situations? What are the possible ways of ensuring that the tomatoes are not wasted, and the farmers are also not at a loss?
items.answer:  Farmers might discard produce if the market price falls below their harvesting/transport costs due to oversupply (too many tomatoes available). items.stem: What are ‘public goods’? shops manufactured by public sector companies

options.label: A
options.text: Goods sold exclusively in government-owned

options.label: B
options.text: Products that are available free of cost

options.label: C
options.text: Services accessible to all members of society

options.label: D
options.text: Items

items.answer:  (C) Services accessible to all members of society Public goods are services or commodities, like public parks, roads, or national defense, that are generally accessible to all members of society. Their use by one person does not typically diminish their availability for others.

items.stem: How does the AGMARK certification differ from the ISI Mark in terms of the products they generally cover? items

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: AGMARK is for agricultural; ISI for industrial

options.label: C
options.text: AGMARK is for imports; ISI for exports only

options.label: D
options.text: Both cover exactly the same product types

items.answer:  (B) AGMARK is for agricultural; ISI for industrial AGMARK is a certification mark for agricultural products in India, ensuring quality standards. The ISI Mark, issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), is generally found on industrial products, ensuring their quality and safety.

items.stem: Which product quality assessment method is correctly paired with its description? appliances produce efficiency level materials

items.answer:  (C) BEE STAR Rating - Indicates energy efficiency level The BEE (Bureau of Energy Efficiency) STAR rating on electronic appliances indicates their energy efficiency. More stars mean the appliance consumes less energy, leading to savings for consumers and environmental benefits.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Governments intervene in markets by implementing regulations like quality standards and price controls. Reason (R) : Such interventions are often necessary to protect consumers, ensure fair practices, and mitigate negative externalities. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Governments play a crucial role in regulating markets. Interventions like setting quality standards and price controls are often implemented to protect consumers from harm or exploitation, ensure fair competition, and address negative side effects of market activities.

items.stem: Which market participant is INCORRECTLY matched with their primary role in the supply chain? sale. consumers. and retailer.

options.label: A
options.text: Manufacturer - Produces the goods for the

options.label: B
options.text: Wholesaler - Sells small quantities to many

options.label: C
options.text: Retailer - Sells to the final end consumer

options.label: D
options.text: Distributor - Bridges gap between wholesaler

items.answer:  (B) Wholesaler - Sells small quantities to many consumers. Wholesalers buy goods in large bulk quantities from manufacturers and primarily sell them in smaller bulk quantities to retailers or other businesses, not directly in small quantities to final consumers.

items.stem: Online markets eliminate the need for any physical goods. NODIA (C) It signifies lower energy consumption, savings (D) It comes with a much longer warranty
items.answer:  (C) It signifies lower energy consumption, savings A higher BEE STAR rating indicates greater energy efficiency. This means the appliance will consume less electricity during its operation, leading to lower electricity bills and long-term cost savings for the consumer.

items.stem: How does an ‘export’ transaction differ fundamentally from an ‘import’ transaction in international trade?

options.label: A
options.text: Export is selling out; import is buying in

options.label: B
options.text: Export is buying in; import is selling out

options.label: C
options.text: Both involve selling goods within one’s

options.label: D
options.text: Both involve only services, not any goods

items.answer:  (A) Export is selling out; import is buying in Exporting involves selling domestically produced goods or services to buyers in foreign countries. Importing involves purchasing goods or services from foreign countries and bringing them into one’s own country for use.

items.stem: Which term is correctly defined in the context of markets? survival.

options.label: A
options.text: Needs - Desires for luxury, non-essential items

options.label: B
options.text: Wants - Basic requirements for human

options.label: C
options.text: Price - Seller’s cost of producing the good

options.label: D
options.text: Trade - Exchange of goods and services

items.answer:  (D) Trade - Exchange of goods and services. Trade is the fundamental economic concept involving the buying, selling, or exchanging of goods and services. Needs are essentials for survival, wants are desires, and price is the agreed exchange value.

items.stem: A family consistently buys groceries from a particular local shopkeeper for many years, even if other shops occasionally offer slightly lower prices. They value the shopkeeper’s friendly service and the ability to buy on credit sometimes. This illustrates : development of non-economic relationships shop

options.label: A
options.text: The purely price-driven nature of all consumer

options.label: B
options.text: The

options.label: C
options.text: The complete absence of competition in local

options.text: The government’s control over where people

items.answer:  (B) The development of non-economic relationships This scenario shows that market interactions can lead to long-term relationships based on trust, personal service, and convenience (like credit), which go beyond purely economic considerations of price alone.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a typical characteristic of the Hampi Bazaar as described by foreign travellers? street

options.label: A
options.text: Trade in a wide variety of goods

options.label: B
options.text: Presence of skilled craftsmen working in

options.label: C

items.answer:  (D) A very small, sparsely supplied local market Foreign travellers like Domingos Paes and Fernao Nuniz described the Hampi Bazaar as a vast, bustling, and exceptionally well-supplied market, trading in a wide array of goods including precious items, not a small or sparsely supplied one.

items.stem: India’s imports from West Asia predominantly include crude petroleum and what other key commodity?

options.label: A
options.text: Software services

options.label: B
options.text: Chemical products

options.label: C

items.answer:  (C) Combines offers from multiple sellers on one An aggregator, in the context of online markets, is a website or mobile application that organizes and combines offers for goods or services from multiple different sellers, presenting them to consumers in a unified platform. items.stem: A pharmaceutical company is found to be selling a substandard drug that poses a health risk to consumers. Which government role is primarily concerned with preventing such a situation from occurring or continuing?

options.label: A
options.text: Providing public goods like parks and roads

options.label: B
options.text: Ensuring quality and safety standards

options.label: C
options.text: Setting minimum prices for agricultural items

options.label: D

items.answer:  (B) Ensuring quality and safety standards The government has a crucial role in setting and enforcing quality and safety standards for products, especially critical ones like medicines. This includes testing and regulations to protect consumer health and safety.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a typical feature or characteristic of a wholesale market?

options.label: A
options.text: Goods are bought in very large quantities

options.label: B
options.text: It primarily sells directly to final consumers

options.label: C
options.text: Products are often stored in godowns

options.label: D
options.text: It serves as a link between producers, retailers

items.answer:  (B) It primarily sells directly to final consumers. Wholesale markets deal in bulk quantities, serving as an intermediary between producers and retailers. They do not typically sell goods in small amounts directly to individual final consumers for their personal use.

items.stem: According to Kautilya’s Arthashastra, traders of ghee were instructed to give buyers a little extra (manasrava) to compensate for what?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost of transporting the measuring can

options.label: B
options.text: Ghee sticking to the measuring can

options.label: C
options.text: The natural evaporation of ghee during trade

options.label: D
options.text: Taxes levied by the king on ghee sale

items.answer:  (B) Ghee sticking to the measuring can Kautilya’s Arthashastra includes a directive that sellers of clarified butter (ghee) should provide a small extra quantity (manasrava) to the buyer. This was to compensate for the amount of ghee that would inevitably stick to the measuring vessel.

items.stem: What does ‘demand’ signify in economics? firm goods

options.label: A
options.text: The total quantity of goods produced by a

options.label: B
options.text: The government’s requirement for public

options.label: C
options.text: Quantity consumers are willing, able to buy

options.label: D
options.text: The seller’s desire to achieve high profits

items.answer:  (C) Quantity consumers are willing, able to buy In economics, demand refers to the quantity of a product or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at various possible prices during a given period of time.

items.stem: How does the role of a ‘distributor’ generally differ from that of a ‘wholesaler’ in a supply chain? from producers retailers physical store goods

items.answer:  (B) Distributors often bridge wholesalers and retailers While wholesalers buy in bulk from producers and sell to retailers, distributors often act as intermediaries who help supply goods from manufacturers or wholesalers to a wider network of retailers, especially when direct reach is difficult.

items.stem: India was the world’s largest importer of _____ oils like palm oil and sunflower oil in 2024.

options.label: A
options.text: essential

options.label: B
options.text: crude

options.label: C
options.text: vegetable

options.label: D

items.stem: How does a ‘godown’ (warehouse) used by a grain wholesaler differ in purpose from a ‘cold storage’ facility? perishables

items.stem: The interactions in markets often move beyond just buying and selling, and can lead to the development of long-lasting _____ between buyers and sellers.

items.stem: When the government sets standards for the quality of medicines, what is its primary aim?

options.label: A
options.text: To increase the profits of drug companies

options.label: B
options.text: To ensure consumer safety and drug efficacy

options.label: C
options.text: To make all medicines available for free

options.label: D
options.text: To limit the number of drugs produced

items.answer:  (B) To ensure consumer safety and drug efficacy By setting and enforcing quality and safety standards for medicines, the government aims to protect public health. This ensures that drugs are effective for their intended use and do not pose undue risks to consumers.

items.stem: A factory producing chemicals releases pollutants into a nearby river, harming the environment and local communities. If the government imposes strict regulations on the factory to control this pollution, it is primarily addressing what aspect of markets?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: The problem of too little competition

options.label: C
options.text: The setting of minimum wages for workers

options.label: D
options.text: The negative external effects of production

items.answer:  (D) The negative external effects of production Pollution from a factory is a negative externality – a cost imposed on third parties (environment, community) not directly involved in the production or consumption of the goods. Government regulation aims to mitigate such harmful external effects.

items.stem: What does ‘supply’ mean in an economic context, regarding goods or services?

items.answer:  (B) The quantity sellers are willing, able to sell Supply in economics refers to the quantity of a product or service that producers or sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at various possible prices during a given period.

items.stem: The Khari Baoli market in Old Delhi is primarily known for trading what kind of commodities?

items.stem: The government’s role in monitoring weights and measures of packaged products primarily aims to achieve what?

items.answer:  (B) To ensure consumers get the correct quantity By monitoring weights and measures, the government aims to protect consumers from unfair trade practices like under-filling of packages. This ensures that consumers receive the net quantity of the product they pay for.

items.stem: How does the function of a ‘manufacturer’ differ from that of a ‘consumer’ in a market? goods goods

items.stem: A consumer is buying a new air conditioner and notices a BEE STAR label with 5 stars on the package. This label primarily helps the consumer assess which quality of the appliance before making the specific purchase?

items.stem: What are ‘external effects’ of markets, and how might the government mitigate them? Use the pollution example.
items.answer:  External effects are impacts beyond the direct transaction (like pollution from factories). The government mitigates negative effects by implementing regulations (e.g., pollution controls, banning harmful products like single-use plastics).

items.stem: Why does the government provide ‘public goods’ like parks or policing?
items.answer:  Private producers are unlikely to provide these goods as they cannot easily charge users or make a profit from them. Since these goods benefit society, the government provides them using public funds.

items.stem: Explain the purpose of the FSSAI mark on food products.
items.answer:  The FSSAI (Food Safety & Standards Authority of India) mark certifies that the food product meets the minimum quality and safety standards set by the government and is safe for consumption.

items.stem: What does the ISI mark signify on products like electrical appliances?
items.answer:  The ISI mark (issued by Bureau of Indian Standards - BIS) signifies that the product conforms to relevant Indian quality standards, ensuring safety and reliability for consumers.

items.stem: What information does the BEE STAR rating provide to consumers?
items.answer:  The BEE STAR rating on appliances indicates energy efficiency. More stars mean the appliance uses less energy/electricity, leading to lower running costs for consumers and less environmental impact.

items.stem: Besides certification marks, how else do consumers assess product quality?
items.answer:  Consumers rely on the product’s or brand’s reputation, often built through word-of-mouth recommendations from friends or relatives. Online reviews and feedback from other users are also increasingly used.

items.stem: What function does negotiation serve in many market transactions?
items.answer:  Negotiation allows buyers and sellers, who may have different initial price expectations, to discuss and bargain until they reach a mutually agreeable price at which the transaction can occur.

items.stem: What makes the Hampi Bazaar historically significant?
items.answer:  It was a major, prosperous trading centre in the powerful Vijayanagara Empire (16th cent.), known for the vast variety of goods traded (grains, silk, gems, animals), as described by foreign travellers like Paes and Nuniz.

items.stem: What is the role of a distributor in the supply chain?
items.answer:  Distributors often act as intermediaries between wholesalers and retailers, especially when distances or terrains make direct supply difficult. They help supply goods from manufacturers/ wholesalers to various retail outlets.

items.stem: Briefly explain the supply chain for online shopping involving an aggregator.
items.answer:  Manufacturers send goods to the aggregator’s warehouse. Consumers order via the aggregator’s platform (app/website). The aggregator processes the order, packs the item, and arranges delivery to the consumer’s doorstep. NODIA CH 12: Understanding Markets

items.stem: Explain how prices are determined in a market through the interaction of buyers and sellers, using the guava example.
items.answer:  Sellers offer goods at a price, buyers decide if it’s acceptable. If prices are too high, few buy; if too low, many want to buy but sellers might lose money. Negotiation leads towards a price balancing supply and demand.

items.stem: Why might vegetables be sold cheaper late at night in a weekly market?
items.answer:  Sellers want to sell off perishable stock before packing up, as vegetables might spoil. Lowering prices late at night attracts last-minute buyers and minimizes losses from unsold goods.

items.stem: Differentiate between a physical market and an online market.
items.answer:  In a physical market, buyers and sellers meet face- to-face at a specific location (shop, stall). In an online market, transactions occur remotely via websites or apps, often without direct personal interaction.

items.stem: What is the difference between a domestic market and an international market?
items.answer:  A domestic market involves buying and selling goods/services within the geographical boundaries of one country. An international market involves trade (exports and imports) between different countries across borders.

items.stem: Explain the role of a wholesaler in the supply chain.
items.answer:  Wholesalers act as intermediaries, buying goods in bulk from manufacturers/producers, storing them (often in godowns or cold storage), and selling them in smaller lots to retailers.

items.stem: What is the role of a retailer in the supply chain?
items.answer:  Retailers buy goods from wholesalers or distributors and sell them in small quantities directly to the final consumers (like households) through shops, stores, or stalls.

items.stem: How does the distribution channel work in online markets involving aggregators?
items.answer:  Manufacturers send products to the aggregator’s warehouse. Consumers order via the aggregator’s app/website. The aggregator packs and delivers the product directly to the consumer.

items.stem: Describe the flow of goods in the Surat textile market example.
items.answer:  Raw cotton comes from farms via mandis. Factories process it (weaving, dyeing) into fabric/ garments. Wholesalers buy finished products, distribute them to retailers across India and internationally for sale to consumers.

items.stem: Besides facilitating economic transactions, what other roles can markets play in society, using the Ima Keithal example?
items.answer:  Markets like Ima Keithal provide significant employment and income opportunities (especially for women in this case). They also act as social and cultural hubs where people from different communities interact, exchange ideas, and share traditions.

items.stem: Give an example of a non-economic tradition observed in some markets.
items.answer:  In South India, sellers of haldi and kumkum often give a small extra quantity free to buyers as a mark of auspiciousness and goodwill, moving beyond purely monetary exchange.

items.stem: Explain one way the government intervenes in markets to control prices.
items.answer:  The government can set maximum prices (price ceilings) on essential goods like medicines to protect consumers, or minimum prices (price floors/MSP) on agricultural products to protect farmers from losses.

items.stem: What are materials or resources used in the production of goods called?
items.answer:  Inputs for production.

items.stem: What is a person or company that makes goods for sale called?
items.answer:  Manufacturer (or producer).

items.stem: What term describes a market where goods are traded within a country’s geographical boundaries?
items.answer:  Domestic market.

items.stem: What term describes selling goods produced in one country to a buyer in another country?
items.answer:  Export.

items.stem: What term describes buying goods from other countries and bringing them into one’s own country?
items.answer:  Import.

items.stem: Who typically buys goods in large quantities from producers and stores them in warehouses or mandis?
items.answer:  Wholesaler.

items.stem: What is a large warehouse used by wholesalers for storing goods called?
items.answer:  Godown.

items.stem: What specialized warehouses maintain low temperatures for perishable goods?
items.answer:  Cold storage.

items.stem: Who sells goods in smaller quantities directly to final consumers like households?
items.answer:  Retailer.

items.stem: What is the term for a website or app that combines offers from multiple sellers for consumers?
items.answer:  Aggregator.

items.stem: Which city in Gujarat is famously known as a textile hub and diamond industry centre?
items.answer:  Surat.

items.stem: What is the unique women-run market in Imphal, Manipur called in the Meitei language?
items.answer:  Ima Keithal (‘Mother’s Market’).

items.stem: What economic concept refers to the quantity consumers are willing to buy at a particular price?
items.answer:  Demand.

items.stem: What economic concept refers to the quantity sellers are willing to sell at a particular price?
items.answer:  Supply.

items.stem: Name one certification mark mentioned that helps consumers assess product quality (e.g., FSSAI, ISI, AGMARK, BEE).
items.answer:  FSSAI/ISI/AGMARK/BEE STAR rating (any one). SSHORT Answer QUESTIO 

items.stem: What are the three essential components required for a place or interaction to be considered a market?
items.answer:  A market requires a buyer, a seller, and an agreement on a price for the exchange of goods or services to take place. NODIA CH 12: Understanding Markets

items.stem: Discuss relationship between markets and prosperity, citing Adam Smith?
items.answer:  Markets facilitate the exchange of goods/services people need but cannot produce themselves. This specialization and trade, according to Adam Smith (and implied throughout), leads to economic activity and prosperity. LONG ANSWER QUESTIO 

items.stem: Analyse the statement : “Markets connect people, traditions, and ideas.”.
items.answer:  Markets are more than economic spaces. Hampi Bazaar showcased diverse goods and craftsmen. Ima Keithal acts as a cultural hub. Junbeel Mela maintains tribal relationships. Shared practices like giving free haldi-kumkum reflect tradition. These interactions within markets facilitate the exchange of not just goods, but also cultural practices and ideas.

items.stem: Analyse how the forces of demand and supply interact to determine the ‘just right’ price in a competitive market, using the guava scenarios.
items.answer:  If supply exceeds demand (seller has many guavas, few buyers at high price), the price tends to fall to attract buyers. If demand exceeds supply (many buyers eager at low price), the price tends to rise as sellers see opportunity. Through negotiation and observing sales, the market gravitates towards an equilibrium price balancing sellers’ need for profit and buyers’ willingness to pay.

items.stem: Compare and contrast the roles and scale of operation of wholesalers and retailers in a typical supply chain.
items.answer:  Wholesalers operate at a larger scale, buying in bulk directly from producers, storing large inventories, and selling large quantities primarily to other businesses (retailers). Retailers operate at a smaller scale, buying smaller lots from wholesalers/distributors and selling individual units directly to end consumers for personal use.

items.stem: Evaluate the pros and cons of online markets compared to physical markets from a consumer’s perspective.
items.answer:  Pros of online : Convenience (shop anytime/ anywhere), wider variety, easy price comparison, home delivery. Cons of online : Cannot physically inspect goods before buying, potential delivery delays/issues, security/privacy concerns, less social interaction. Physical markets offer immediate purchase, inspection, and social interaction but less convenience/variety.

items.stem: Evaluate the pros and cons of online markets compared to physical markets from a seller’s perspective.
items.answer:  Pros of online : Access to a wider customer base (geographically), lower overheads (no physical store needed), easier inventory management. Cons of online : High competition, reliance on platform/aggregator, logistics/delivery costs and complexities, difficulty building personal customer relationships, challenges in showcasing product quality digitally.

items.stem: Analyse the government’s role in regulating markets. Why is intervention sometimes necessary, and what are the potential downsides of excessive regulation?
items.answer:  Government intervenes to ensure fairness (price controls), protect consumers (quality/safety standards), mitigate negative externalities (pollution), ensure availability of public goods, and maintain economic stability. However, excessive regulation can stifle innovation, increase costs for businesses, reduce market efficiency, and potentially lead to shortages if price controls are poorly set.

items.stem: “Consumer protection mechanisms like quality certifications (FSSAI, ISI) and online reviews empower buyers.” Analyse how these tools help consumers make informed decisions.
items.answer:  Certifications provide standardized assurance from authorities that a product meets minimum quality/safety levels, reducing risk for consumers. Online reviews offer peer experiences regarding product performance, quality, and seller reliability. Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart Both provide valuable information beyond seller claims, empowering consumers to choose products more confidently and avoid substandard goods.

items.stem: Analyse the economic and social significance of markets like Ima Keithal, run entirely by women.
items.answer:  Economically, Ima Keithal provides crucial livelihood and financial independence for thousands of women vendors and their families. Socially, it represents a powerful space for women’s collective organization, economic empowerment, preserving traditional crafts/attire, and serves as a significant cultural centre for the community in Imphal.

items.stem: Considering the Surat example, analyse how geographical location, historical factors, and infrastructure contribute to the development of a major trading hub.
items.answer:  Surat’s west coast location facilitated port development and maritime trade historically. Proximity to cotton-growing regions provided raw materials. Development of transport infrastructure (highways, railways) connected it inland. The presence of skilled artisan communities with skills passed down generations created expertise (textiles, diamonds), making it a thriving hub.

items.stem: How do markets reflect consumer preferences and potentially drive innovation, using the energy- efficient refrigerator example?
items.answer:  When many consumers demand a certain feature (like energy efficiency), retailers communicate this demand back through the supply chain (wholesalers to producers). Producers, seeing a market opportunity or responding to demand signals, innovate and adapt their products (making energy-efficient models) to meet consumer preferences, benefiting society.

items.stem: Analyse the concept of ‘public goods’. Why are markets generally inefficient at providing them?
items.answer:  Public goods (like clean air, national defense, public parks) are typically non-excludable (hard to prevent anyone from using them) and non- rivalrous (one person’s use doesn’t diminish availability for others). Private firms find it difficult to charge users for such goods, making them unprofitable to supply through the market mechanism alone.

items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for agricultural products as a government intervention. What are the intended benefits and potential drawbacks?
items.answer:  Intended benefit : Protect farmers from price crashes due to bumper harvests or market manipulation, ensuring a minimum income. Potential drawbacks : Can lead to overproduction of supported crops, requires costly government procurement and storage, may distort market prices, and benefits might not always reach small/ marginal farmers effectively.

items.stem: Analyse the importance of trust and relationships in market interactions, even in a monetary economy.
items.answer:  While money facilitates exchange, trust remains crucial. Long-term relationships with local vendors (tailor, grocer allowing monthly credit) build reliability and personalized service. Reputation (word-of-mouth) influences buying decisions. Even online, seller ratings build trust. These non-price factors significantly shape market interactions and consumer loyalty.

items.stem: How might international trade (imports/exports) impact a domestic market for a specific product (e.g., vegetable oils in India)?
items.answer:  Imports (like large amounts of vegetable oil into India) increase the total supply available in the domestic market, which generally leads to lower prices for consumers. It can also create competition for domestic producers. Exports create demand for domestically produced goods in other countries, potentially raising domestic prices but benefiting producers.

items.stem: Considering the evolution from barter to digital money, analyse the changing nature of ‘trust’ in economic transactions.
items.answer:  Barter required direct trust between individuals. Commodity money needed trust in the commodity’s value. items.stem: A farmer brings freshly harvested mangoes to a wholesale mandi. Buyer A offers `30/kg, wanting 100 kgs for retail shops. Buyer B offers `35/kg, needing only 20 kgs for a fruit juice stall. Buyer C, a large exporter, offers `28/kg but wants to buy the entire lot of 500 kgs immediately. Evaluate the farmer’s options. (i) Who are the different types of buyers in this wholesale market scenario? (ii) What are the pros and cons for the farmer of selling to Buyer C (the exporter)? (iii) What strategy might the farmer adopt to maximize income while minimizing risk?
items.answer:  (i) Buyer A is likely a retailer or distributor supplying shops. Buyer B is a small-scale direct consumer/processor. Buyer C is a large-scale buyer, possibly for export or major distribution. (ii) Pro : Sells the entire stock quickly, avoids storage/spoilage risk, immediate bulk payment. Con : Gets the lowest price per kg (`28) compared to other offers. (iii) The farmer might try negotiating a slightly higher price with Buyer C, or sell smaller quantities to Buyers A and B at higher prices first, offer the remaining bulk to Buyer C, balancing higher price potential with the risk of unsold stock.

items.stem: You want to buy a new electric kettle. You check online reviews : Brand X has excellent reviews for durability but is expensive. Brand Y is cheaper but has mixed reviews about lifespan. You visit a local store; the retailer recommends Brand Z, which has an ISI mark and a 3-star BEE rating, priced moderately. (i) What does the ISI mark on Brand Z indicate? (ii) What does the 3-star BEE rating tell you about Brand Z’s energy consumption? (iii) Evaluate which kettle might be the best choice, considering price, quality signals (reviews, certifications), and energy efficiency.
items.answer:  (i) The ISI mark indicates that Brand Z meets the minimum quality and safety standards set by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). (ii) It indicates moderate energy efficiency – it uses less electricity than lower-rated models but more than higher-rated (4 or 5-star) models. (iii) Brand X offers high quality but at high cost. Brand Y is cheap but risky due to mixed reviews. Brand Z offers a balance : moderate price, assured safety/quality (ISI mark), and reasonable energy efficiency (3-star BEE). Brand Z appears a sensible choice balancing cost, quality, and running expense.

items.stem: The government observes that due to a severe drought, the market price of lentils (dal), an essential food item, has tripled, causing hardship for poor families. They are considering interventions. Option 1 : Set a maximum retail price (price ceiling) significantly below the current market price. Option 2 : Release buffer stocks of lentils into the market. (i) What is the intended benefit of Option 1 (price ceiling)? (ii) What is a potential negative consequence of setting the price ceiling too low (Option 1)? (iii) Evaluate Option 2 (releasing buffer stocks) as an alternative intervention.
items.answer:  (i) The intended benefit is to make lentils affordable for consumers, especially poor families, by legally limiting how high the price can go. (ii) If the price ceiling is below the production/ procurement cost, sellers/producers might refuse to sell, leading to shortages, black markets, or reduced future production. (iii) Releasing buffer stocks increases the supply of lentils in the market. Increased supply naturally tends to lower the market price without direct price fixing, making it affordable while avoiding the potential shortages associated with strict price ceilings. This is often a more market-friendly approach. NODIA Part - 2 Based on Exploring Society : India and Beyond NODIA

items.stem: A handicraft cooperative in a rural area makes unique bamboo products. They struggle to sell them locally as demand is low. An e-commerce platform (aggregator) offers to list their products online, handle payments, and arrange shipping for a commission fee, reaching customers nationwide. (i) What type of market access does the e-commerce platform provide to the cooperative? (ii) Identify one major benefit for the cooperative of using this online platform. (iii) Evaluate one potential challenge the cooperative might face when selling through this online aggregator model.
items.answer:  (i) It provides access to a much wider domestic market (potentially international too), connecting them with consumers far beyond their limited local reach. (ii) A major benefit is significantly increased market exposure and potential customer base, leading to higher sales opportunities for their unique products. (iii) Challenges could include : paying commission fees reducing their profit margin, difficulty competing with numerous other sellers online, managing packaging/shipping logistics, or dependence on the platform’s policies and visibility algorithms.

items.stem: A factory producing chemicals is located near a residential area. While it provides local employment, residents complain about polluted air and water discharge affecting their health and the local environment. The factory management argues they follow basic regulations. (i) What kind of market failure or ‘external effect’ does this situation represent? (ii) What role should the government play in this situation ? (iii) Evaluate the conflict between economic activity (factory employment) and environmental/social well-being in this case.
items.answer:  (i) This represents a negative externality, where the factory’s production process imposes costs (pollution, health impacts) on third parties (residents, environment) not directly involved in the buying or selling of the chemicals. (ii) The government’s role is to intervene by understanding the negative effects, setting stricter environmental regulations for the factory (beyond basic ones if needed), monitoring compliance, and potentially imposing penalties to mitigate the pollution and protect public health/environment. (iii) There is a clear conflict. The factory provides economic benefits (jobs, production), but its operations harm the environment and residents’ health. Effective government regulation aims to find a balance, allowing economic activity while minimizing harmful external effects, ensuring sustainable development rather than prioritizing profit over well-being. wwww.nodia.i  Click Here to Buy book on Amazon
